{"task": {"id": "I_kwDOVRkquM8AAAABinWmlQ", "item_id": "PVTI_lAHOAHSLSM4Bn_T5zhL99SQ", "project_id": "PVT_kwHOAHSLSM4Bn_T5", "number": 180, "title": "Add multiple SRAM save profiles and persistent screenshot-based save states", "body": "## Goal

Add two complementary ways to save and resume a game in the browser emulator:

1. **Save data**: multiple independent game-native SRAM saves for the same cartridge.
2. **Save state / Load state**: emulator-level snapshots that restore the game at the saved moment, even for cartridges with no in-game save feature.

The maintainer wants both features, not just SRAM management or a single quick-save slot. Prefer an expandable, screenshot-based history over a fixed set of 3/10/100 numbered slots. Keep the existing cartridge-centered player UI simple.

Baseline inspected: `main` at `3ee93a124f266312a84a4d2ef464c94f4660d110`. The current [web/app.js](https://github.com/takahirox/snes-rust/blob/main/web/app.js) stores one battery-backed SRAM payload under `snes-rust:sram:<normalized ROM SHA-256>`, and the ROM library uses IndexedDB. The core has separate CPU, SystemBus, PPU, APU/SPC700 and DSP state; [snes-wasm exports](https://github.com/takahirox/snes-rust/blob/main/crates/snes-wasm/src/lib.rs) expose SRAM but do not yet expose full machine snapshots.

## 1. Multiple game-native save data profiles

- For each supported battery-backed cartridge, provide independently selectable SRAM profiles, initially **Save 1**. Make the selected profile visible near the inserted-cartridge information, rather than adding another large management screen.
- Support creating a fresh profile (normal cartridge initialization), selecting an existing profile, duplicating the current SRAM, and deleting a profile. Use simple default names such as Save 1, Save 2, etc. Show useful last-save timestamps. No arbitrary small slot limit; storage capacity is the practical limit.
- Scope profiles by normalized ROM SHA-256 and stable profile ID, not filename, title or ROM source. Identical local/bundled/library ROM bytes and copier-header variants retain the same identity. Different ROM revisions must not silently share SRAM.
- Remember the selected profile per ROM across reloads. Switching to another profile saves the outgoing SRAM first, validates the incoming SRAM, then resets/restarts the same ROM with the selected data; never hot-swap SRAM into an unrelated running game state. Respect hidden-tab suspension and existing error/restore gates. Selecting the already active profile does not reset the game.
- Reset continues to reset volatile machine state and retain the active profile's SRAM. Keep the current automatic persistence triggers, cancellation behavior and storage-error warnings.
- Preserve existing users' SRAM. Treat the legacy single-ROM save as Save 1, with an idempotent, failure-safe migration or direct reuse of its key. Verify the original bytes before removing anything; do not leave redundant compatibility mechanisms unnecessarily. A failed migration must not result in an apparently empty save or overwrite.
- Removing a ROM library entry must not delete its profiles or states. Reimporting the same ROM restores access to its existing data.
- No SRAM selector is needed for games without supported battery-backed SRAM. Such games still support emulator save states.
- Avoid silently deleting dependent save states when deleting a profile. Provide an explicit destructive-action policy and clear confirmation for affected data; do not strand states or allow an active profile's automatic persistence to recreate a deleted save.

## 2. Full machine save/load state in Rust and Wasm

Implement a versioned binary snapshot format and safe APIs at the Rust core level, then expose the same functionality through the Wasm interface. A state is not just SRAM, a screenshot, or a controller replay.

Capture enough state to continue the exact emulated execution deterministically:

- 65C816 registers/flags/program counter, execution state and any observable counters.
- WRAM, SRAM, cartridge mapping/identity metadata, bus/open-bus state, I/O, controller latch and polling state.
- PPU registers, VRAM, CGRAM, OAM, latches, timing/raster position, framebuffer geometry and retained frame output, pending/latched state that affects subsequent rendering.
- SPC700 registers and RAM, APU ports, clock/cycle debt, timer phases, boot/upload/pending commands, DSP voices/envelopes/BRR history/interpolation, noise, echo/filter state, and any other state that influences subsequent audio.
- DMA/HDMA, CPU math, IRQ/NMI, scheduling/event counters and other necessary hardware-visible state.

Choose a well-defined stable execution boundary (prefer the existing completed field/frame boundary, including appropriate synchronization of deferred PPU/APU work). Support saving while paused without advancing the guest or changing its playback intent. Preserve any cached/latched data that affects emulation; discard/rebuild only demonstrably derived acceleration structures. Do not blindly serialize raw Rust memory, pointers, host resources, or optimizer scratch state. Recent event-driven timing, polling-loop skipping, fast memory maps, deferred APU and scanline rendering must continue to work correctly after restore.

- Keep the ROM bytes external to snapshots: bind snapshots to their exact ROM hash, and validate that the loaded cartridge matches. Do not duplicate ROM bytes in every state.
- Use explicit format/version, integrity checks and bounded parsing/decompression. Validate lengths, ranges, enums and state invariants. Reject incompatible, corrupt, oversized or wrong-ROM files safely. Keep the current machine and data intact if validation fails. A state from an unsupported future/older version must show actionable feedback rather than partially restore. Maintain a documented format/version policy; no promise of universal compatibility with future emulator revisions or other emulators.
- Make load atomic from the user's perspective: decode/validate into a candidate before committing; preserve the currently inserted cartridge and active save data on failure. Keep native and Wasm implementations consistent. A successful restore must not reset or reinitialize the guest.
- After loading, discard obsolete queued Web Audio buffers, render the restored framebuffer, clear stale physical keyboard/touch input, reconcile guest controller state safely, and reset wall-clock frame pacing. Resume the loaded moment when visible and gameplay is intended; respect explicit manual Pause and automatic hidden-tab suspension. Do not restore host volume/mute, CRT/Pixel preferences, fullscreen, focus, DOM state or wall-clock timestamps as part of the emulated machine.

## 3. SRAM safety when loading a state

A complete save state includes SRAM at capture time, which may be older than the active profile's currently persisted SRAM. Loading it must not silently erase more recent progress.

- Scope each state to its ROM and originating SRAM profile (for non-battery games, use a ROM-level state history without exposing artificial SRAM profiles).
- Before restoring an older SRAM image into the profile, safely persist the current recoverable SRAM and preserve a **user-accessible recovery copy** if the bytes would change. A simple recovery entry in the save-data picker, with timestamp, is acceptable; the exact UX may be refined. Do not create redundant backups for identical SRAM. The user must be able to recover the pre-load SRAM through the ordinary UI without developer tools.
- Restore the saved machine and SRAM consistently; do not simply substitute today's SRAM into a historical snapshot and claim exact restoration.
- If backup/persistence or validation fails, do not commit a destructive state load. Keep the prior guest and persisted save recoverable. Consider transaction ordering across IndexedDB and any existing localStorage records, including interruption/reload. Provide a clear error and retry path.
- Never cross-write another profile or ROM. Ensure subsequent autosaves target the correct active profile; profile switching and loading are serialized so stale asynchronous operations cannot write to the wrong record.

## 4. Persistent save state history and UI

- Add readily visible **Save state** and **Load state** actions in the player controls beneath the screen. Keep Save data selection with the cartridge information. Preserve existing minimal header, Play/Pause, Reset, volume, display controls, fullscreen and all twelve touch controls.
- Each Save state action creates a new durable snapshot, rather than overwriting a fixed slot by default. Store compressed binary snapshots and associated metadata in IndexedDB (reuse the existing storage architecture where appropriate). Store a thumbnail from the actual captured game framebuffer, not a generic or fabricated image. Use compact thumbnails and timestamped stable identifiers; actual emulated play time may be displayed if reliable.
- Load state opens a compact, scrollable history for the current ROM/profile, newest first, showing real screenshot thumbnails and timestamps. Selecting an entry restores it; provide a separate accessible Remove action. No artificial 100-slot cap, no automatic eviction of user saves to maintain a fixed count, and no empty numbered slots. Validate at least 100 saved states per ROM/profile and larger collections where practical.
- Read metadata/thumbnails on demand or in pages; avoid reading every snapshot into memory or decoding all state payloads at startup. Avoid unnecessary UI/frame stalls and storage duplication. Save operations must capture immutable state at the user's requested boundary, not race with later frames or cartridge changes.
- No upload, account, cloud service, large settings screen, or new permanent explanation panel. Browser storage can be denied, exhausted or cleared: handle failures truthfully without claiming successful saves or deleting other states; normal gameplay and ROM selection remain usable. Keep a failed operation's recoverable data intact.
- Preserve UI/UX principles: Keep it simple; Show, don't tell; Intuitive and predictable. Use responsive wrapping, accessible keyboard/touch navigation, focus management and safe-area-aware scrolling. Keep gameplay view the primary focus.

## 5. File backup and portability

Add import/export after the core and persistent UI are working. Support downloading/importing raw SRAM files for the appropriate ROM/profile and exporting/importing the project's versioned save-state files (with ROM identity and format metadata, but without ROM content). Validate all inputs, avoid implicit overwrites, and provide a concise compatibility/error message. Import must use the same safe validation/backup path, with no assumption that third-party emulator save-state formats are compatible. Document limitations. This can be a later PR under this umbrella, rather than blocking useful earlier milestones.

## Implementation sequence

Use multiple focused PRs if helpful. Do not close this umbrella simply because SRAM profiles or a native serialization API alone are implemented.

1. Multiple SRAM profiles, migration and switching safety.
2. Native Rust snapshot encoding/decoding, deterministic round-trip tests and corrupt-input safety.
3. Wasm snapshot API, integration with current player lifecycle and non-destructive SRAM restore.
4. IndexedDB history, actual thumbnails, Save state / Load state UI and large-collection tests.
5. Import/export and complete documentation/validation.

Keep internal APIs and storage schema coherent; avoid speculative frameworks, unnecessary shims and per-game special cases. User data compatibility matters, but do not retain obsolete implementation paths merely in anticipation of hypothetical future needs.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Existing single-ROM SRAM saves survive upgrade without data loss. Multiple profiles of the same ROM remain isolated through save, switch, reset, duplication, deletion, reload, removal/reimport and same-ROM identity variants. Existing SRAM recovery safeguards remain effective.
- [ ] Native and Wasm round trips restore deterministic guest state and output. For fixed input sequences after a snapshot, compare the continued CPU/bus/PPU/APU/DSP state, video digests, audio samples and SRAM with uninterrupted execution. Include ordinary LoROM/HiROM, both demos, battery and non-battery games, high resolution/Mode 7, DMA/HDMA, timers, interrupts, deferred APU and optimized event scheduling. Test snapshots during complex gameplay, not just at the title screen.
- [ ] Invalid, truncated, tampered, wrong-ROM, unsupported-version and oversized snapshot/import inputs are rejected without partial restore, save loss, runaway allocation or host crash. Verify clean recovery. Test interrupted writes, quota/unavailable IndexedDB, failed legacy migration, stale loads and overlapping operations.
- [ ] Loading an older state restores its exact machine/SRAM state, with a recoverable pre-load copy when necessary. Verify backup failure blocks destructive load, profile isolation, no cross-ROM writes and recovery via visible UI.
- [ ] Save/load while playing and manually paused, hidden/visible transitions, fresh audio, no stale input, unchanged volume/display/fullscreen, and correct Reset behavior. Test both bundled and saved/local ROM sources and no-SRAM games.
- [ ] Save at least 100 distinct snapshots, reload browser, browse and load arbitrary earlier entries, remove entries, verify actual matching thumbnails and stable IDs. No forced overwrites or eager loading of all payloads. Measure save/load latency and storage size on representative workloads; no unjustified performance regression in normal gameplay.
- [ ] Validate import/export round trips for SRAM and the project's own state format. Never export ROM bytes or upload user files. Document storage scope, compatibility and backup guidance.
- [ ] Test actual production Wasm and browser UI across desktop, narrow portrait and short landscape, with keyboard and touch. Preserve cartridge library, all twelve controls, existing display/audio behavior and Pages subpath/asset constraints.
- [ ] Run required Rust, diagnostic, browser and production build/CI gates with meaningful assertions intact. Record exact results, benchmark implications, limitations and optional checks not run. Keep [README](https://github.com/takahirox/snes-rust/blob/main/README.md) concise and accurate.

## Post-merge verification

For each user-visible milestone, verify the corresponding Pages deployment after merge. At completion, test the published app with a permitted battery-backed game and a non-battery game: create two profiles, save multiple states, reload, restore an earlier state, verify SRAM recovery and export/import. Record actual revision, workflow and browser results. Track confirmed publication regressions separately; do not require post-merge checks before merge.

Related: #122 (cartridge/SRAM lifecycle), #170 (IndexedDB ROM library), #176 (visibility suspension/resumption), #174 (performance optimization).
